Syllabus

Catalog description

Exploring multidimensional data. Discovering structure in data. Bootstrapping basics and dependent data. Data partitioning. Statistical pattern recognition: classifiers and clustering. Bivariate and multivariate smoothing. Nonparametric regression models. Advanced topics in Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).

Course objectives

This course provides a rigorous foundation in computational statistics, combining theory with applied research practice. It covers key methods such as MCMC, EM, bootstrap, importance sampling, optimization, and simulation techniques, emphasizing both their theoretical basis and practical implementation for complex statistical challenges. It also trains students to assess algorithm efficiency and scalability in high-dimensional or large-data contexts, and to apply these tools in an independent, project-based research setting that culminates in clear and professional scholarly communication.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Explain and apply advanced computational algorithms (MCMC, EM, importance sampling, bootstrap, optimization, numerical integration) to complex statistical models.
  2. Implement and evaluate statistical computing methods in appropriate languages (R, Python, or C++), ensuring both accuracy and efficiency.
  3. Critically analyze algorithm performance in terms of convergence, stability, scalability, and suitability for high-dimensional or large-scale problems.
  4. Compare and justify methodological choices by linking algorithmic properties with theoretical foundations in statistical inference.
  5. Design and conduct simulation studies to assess the robustness and reliability of computational methods.
  6. Collaborate on interdisciplinary research projects using real-world datasets from diverse domains.
  7. Communicate statistical findings effectively.

Prerequisites and background

The catalog lists no formal prerequisites. Students are, however, expected to have working knowledge of Python, R, and SQL, including experience with relational databases. These topics are not taught in the course.

Instructional methods

The course combines lectures, hands-on computational exercises, and an individual research-oriented data analysis project. Each student selects a topic in computational statistics, identifies a suitable dataset, carries out an independent analysis through the semester, and prepares a draft research paper.

Students use R and Python. Each student maintains their own GitHub repository and gives the instructor access. Assignments and project materials are managed through GitHub and ODTUClass.

Grading

Deliverable Points
Participation / Discussion 10
Homework 20
Midterm 30
Final Paper 40
Total 100

Policies

Attendance. At least 70% of scheduled sessions must be attended. Attendance and engagement count toward the Participation/Discussion grade. Students below 70% receive an NA (Not Attended) grade regardless of other results.

Late submissions. Late submissions are not accepted. All assignments and the final paper are due by their stated deadlines.

Make-ups. Make-up exams are not offered.

Devices. Mobile phone use is not allowed in lectures.

Students with disabilities. Students who need academic adjustments or auxiliary aids should contact the ODTU Disability Support Office and/or the instructor, and the advisor of students with disabilities in their department, as soon as possible.

Academic honesty. All members of the METU community are bound by the METU Honour Code: to embrace only the success and recognition they deserve, and to act with integrity in their use, evaluation and presentation of facts, data and documents.
